<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

display.text:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Run Ruff Lint (no auto-fix)
        run: uv run ruff check .

      - name: Verify Ruff Formatting (no auto-fix)
        run: uv run ruff format --check .

  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Run Mypy (core)
        run: uv run --directory core mypy .

      - name: Run Mypy (mcp_server)
        run: uv run --directory mcp_server mypy .

      - name: Run Mypy (local_server)
        run: uv run --directory local_server mypy .

      - name: Run Mypy (cli)
        run: uv run --directory cli mypy .

      - name: Run Mypy (client)
        run: uv run --directory client mypy .

      - name: Run Mypy (connectors)
        run: uv run --directory connectors mypy .

  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: Run Bandit
        run: uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src local_server/src cli/src client/src connectors/src

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}

      - name: Pytest (core)
        run: uv run --directory core pytest --cov=core --cov-report=term-missing
        env:
          COVERAGE_FILE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.core

      - name: Pytest (mcp_server)
        run: uv run --directory mcp_server pytest --cov=mcp_server --cov-report=term-missing
        env:
          COVERAGE_FILE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.mcp_server

      - name: Pytest (local_server)
        run: uv run --directory local_server pytest --cov=local_server --cov-report=term-missing
        env:
          COVERAGE_FILE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.local_server

      - name: Pytest (cli)
        run: uv run --directory cli pytest --cov=cli --cov-report=term-missing
        env:
          COVERAGE_FILE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.cli

      - name: Pytest (client)
        run: uv run --directory client pytest --cov=client --cov-report=term-missing
        env:
          COVERAGE_FILE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.client

      - name: Pytest (connectors)
        run: uv run --directory connectors pytest --cov=connectors --cov-report=term-missing
        env:
          COVERAGE_FILE: ${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.connectors

      - name: Combine and report coverage
        run: |
          unset COVERAGE_FILE
          uv run coverage combine \
            "${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.core" \
            "${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.mcp_server" \
            "${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.local_server" \
            "${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.cli" \
            "${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.client" \
            "${{ github.workspace }}/.coverage.connectors"
          uv run coverage xml -o "${{ github.workspace }}/coverage.xml"
          uv run coverage report

      - name: Upload coverage report
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage-${{ matrix.python-version }}
          path: coverage.xml
          if-no-files-found: error

  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, typecheck, security, test]
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      - name: CLI reports a version
        run: |
          version="$(uv run python -m cli --version)"
          [ -n "$version" ]
          echo "OK: $version"

      - name: CLI exposes connectors commands
        run: |
          help="$(uv run python -m cli connectors --help)"
          echo "$help" | grep -q list
          echo "$help" | grep -q ingest
          echo "OK: connectors help"

      - name: MCP server boots and serves /mcp
        run: |
          uv run python -m mcp_server > /tmp/mcp_server.log 2>&1 &
          SERVER_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -sfX POST http://localhost:8000/mcp \
              -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
              -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1,"params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"ci","version":"1"}}}' \
              -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          kill "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          wait "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "MCP server did not respond on :8000/mcp"
            cat /tmp/mcp_server.log
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "OK: MCP server responded with 200"

      - name: python -m client.run brings up both services and stops cleanly
        run: |
          uv run python -m client.run > /tmp/clientrun.log 2>&1 &
          RUN_PID=$!
          probe() {
            curl -sf -o /dev/null http://localhost:8501 &&
              curl -sfX POST http://localhost:8000/mcp \
                -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
                -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"initialize","id":1,"params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"ci","version":"1"}}}' \
                -o /dev/null
          }
          ok=0
          for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
            if probe; then ok=1; break; fi
            sleep 1
          done
          if [ "$ok" -ne 1 ]; then
            echo "client.run did not bring up both services"
            cat /tmp/clientrun.log
            kill "$RUN_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
            exit 1
          fi
          kill -INT "$RUN_PID"
          wait "$RUN_PID"
          echo "OK: both services stopped cleanly"

  ci-green:
    name: CI green
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, typecheck, security, test, smoke]
    if: always()
    steps:
      - name: Verify all required jobs succeeded
        run: |
          results='${{ join(needs.*.result, ' ') }}'
          echo "Job results: $results"
          for result in $results; do
            if [ "$result" != "success" ]; then
              echo "::error::A required job did not succeed ($results)"
              exit 1
            fi
          done
          echo "OK: all required jobs succeeded"

Let me think through the recommended design carefully.

### Bundling approach
For a Python CLI → self-contained single binary across Linux/macOS/Windows, the pragmatic SOTA-ish choice is **PyInstaller `--onefile`**. Alternatives: Nuitka (faster, smaller-ish, more fragile builds, longer CI), PyOxidizer (stale), shiv/pex/zipapp (need Python present → not truly self-contained).

Given fastmcp/pydantic (Rust pydantic-core extension!), PyInstaller can bundle pydantic-core. Actually pydantic v2 uses pydantic-core compiled wheels — PyInstaller handles them via hooks. fastmcp pulls many packages; PyInstaller hooks may need curation. There's real risk. I should flag: build a spike first to validate that PyInstaller bundles fastmcp cleanly.

Startup time: onefile extracts to temp dir each run → slow startup (~1s+). SOTA CLIs are instant. For a better experience, use **onedir** packaged as a tar/zip archive, and the install script extracts it. But then self-update = replace directory. Or use onefile but note the startup cost. Trade-off.

Actually, a cleaner modern approach: **distribute a self-contained "onedir" bundle as an archive**, OR onefile. Let me recommend onefile for simplicity first, with a note about onedir if startup matters.

Hmm, but "single binary" is what user asked. onefile gives single binary. Let me recommend onefile and mention the temp-extraction startup cost and the option to mitigate.

Consider also: **Astral's `uv` + `python-build-standalone`** approach used by e.g. some tools — ship an archive containing a python + installed venv + launcher script. Not single file though.

I'll recommend PyInstaller onefile as primary, Nuitka as a fallback if size/speed/AV problems.

### Version embedding
- Single source of truth. Use git tag → set version at build time. Options: `hatch-vcs` (derives from git tags) or pass `--version` into PyInstaller via a generated module. Since version.py hardcodes 0.1.0, recommend switching to a build-time injected version (env var PYINSTALLER + a generated `_build_info.py`), or use `importlib.metadata` (works in PyInstaller with the dist-info). Simplest: CI passes the tag; a build step writes version. Also embed update metadata.
- Also embed build commit, date for `--version --verbose`.

### Release/tagging CI
Currently no tags, versions hardcoded 0.1.0 across 6 packages. Recommend:
- **release-please** (Google) — Conventional Commits → opens a "release PR" that bumps version + changelog; merging creates the git tag + GitHub Release. This is the SOTA default and works with monorepo (can do single root release).
- Alternative: **semantic-release** (Node) or **python-semantic-release** (native Python, tags + PyPI).
- For a uv workspace monorepo, release-please with a single component is simplest. Multi-package versioning is complexity we probably don't need → tag the whole repo as one product version.

Flow:
1. Merge PRs with Conventional Commit messages into main.
2. release-please maintains a release PR (bumps version, CHANGELOG).
3. Merge release PR → creates tag `vX.Y.Z` and a GitHub Release (draft).
4. Tag triggers `release.yml` matrix build (6 targets) → builds binaries → uploads assets + `checksums.txt` to the Release → publishes it.

### Build matrix
`release.yml`, triggered on `push: tags: ['v*']` (or release-please output). Matrix:
- ubuntu-latest → linux-x86_64
- ubuntu-24.04-arm → linux-arm64 (GitHub now has arm64 runners) OR use cross/QEMU
- macos-13 → macos-x86_64
- macos-14 → macos-arm64
- windows-latest → windows-x86_64
Build with `uv sync` + `pyinstaller cli/src/cli/__main__.py` (entry via a spec file). Name assets: `agentic-odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>[.exe]`. Generate SHA256 `checksums.txt`. Code-sign macOS (ad-hoc or Developer ID + notarization) — unsigned binaries get Gatekeeper-blocked. Windows signing optional but recommended (SmartScreen).

### Install script (`install.sh`)
`curl -fsSL https://.../install.sh | sh`:
- Detect OS/arch (uname).
- Query GitHub API for latest release (or a stable `releases/latest/download/` URL).
- Download the matching asset.
- Verify checksum from `checksums.txt`.
- Install to `~/.local/bin` (or `/usr/local/bin`) — respect `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR`.
- Update PATH hint + shell completion install.
Also a `install.ps1` for Windows: `irm ... | iex`.

### Self-update mechanism
Design:
- A `cli/update.py` module with:
  - `check_for_update()` — hits GitHub Releases latest, compares semver against embedded `__version__`.
  - `perform_update()` — download asset for current platform, verify checksum, atomically replace the running executable (`os.replace`), set exec bit. On Windows, a running .exe can't be overwritten → spawn a helper that waits for exit, replaces, deletes temp (common pattern; or use a `.new` + rename on next launch).

+# Bundled CLI Distribution & Self-Update — Design
+
+Date: 2026-10-15
+Status: Approved (design); implementation plan pending
+
+## Intent and why
+
+Today the `agentic-odi` CLI is consumed by installing the whole `uv`
+workspace in editable mode. We want a world-class, "state-of-the-art"
+binary distribution: a self-contained executable that a user installs with
+a single `curl … | sh` and that keeps itself current without the user
+managing a Python toolchain.
+
+This mirrors the experience of `gh`, `deno`, `bun`, and `ollama`: install
+with a one-liner, get a native-feeling command, and receive updates without
+thinking about it.
+
+## Goals
+
+- A self-contained artifact per platform with **near-instant startup**.
+- One-line install: `curl -fsSL <url>/install.sh | sh` (and a PowerShell
+  equivalent for Windows).
+- **Automatic background updates, on by default**, plus an explicit
+  user-invoked update command.
+- Automated versioning and release/tag creation driven by CI.
+- Support Linux (x86_64, arm64), macOS (x86_64, arm64), Windows (x86_64).
+
+## Non-goals
+
+- Code signing / notarization (deferred; document the workarounds).
+- Packaging the MCP server / local server / chat client as binaries (this is
+  about the CLI only).
+- Publishing to PyPI as the primary distribution channel.
+- A vanity download domain (use GitHub Releases for now).
+
+## Anti-goals (what would make this a failure even if it "works")
+
+- Shipping a build that crashes on `--backend mcp` because a dependency was
+  stripped for size.
+- An auto-updater that blocks or slows a command when offline.
+- An updater that can corrupt an install if interrupted (non-atomic swap).
+- Replacing a running executable in place (fails on Windows; races on unix).
+
+## Constraints
+
+- The CLI is a Python package (`agentic-odi-cli`) in a `uv` workspace with
+  six members. Once bundled, the CLI no longer depends on the workspace at
+  runtime; the source tree keeps its current editable-install workflow.
+- **Correction found during design review:** although a `LocalBackend` exists
+  (`cli/src/cli/backend.py`), every `outcomes` command currently hardcodes the
+  MCP backend (`get_backend("mcp", …)`, and `score` calls `_call_mcp`
+  directly). `LocalBackend` is unreachable and there is no `--backend` flag.
+  So the CLI as shipped effectively requires a running MCP server. Wiring the
+  local backend up and exposing `--backend {local,mcp}` is **in scope** (see
+  Decision 7) so the binary is genuinely useful standalone.
+- The CLI imports `fastmcp` at module top (`cli/src/cli/outcomes.py`), which
+  pulls a large tree (mcp, httpx, starlette, uvicorn). `pydantic` v2 pulls
+  compiled `pydantic-core`. These are the bundling risk points.
+- No git tags exist today; `cli/src/cli/version.py` hardcodes `0.1.0`.
+- Reproduction of the current runner matrix: GitHub-hosted Ubuntu, macOS,
+  and Windows runners.
+
+## Decisions (made by the human partner unless noted)
+
+1. **Bundler: PyInstaller `--onedir`, shipped as a compressed archive.**
+   `--onefile` re-extracts to a temp dir on every invocation and adds
+   ~0.5–1.5s startup latency; `--onedir` starts near-instantly. We accept
+   "one downloadable archive, installed into a versioned directory" instead
+   of "one literal file." Nuitka is the fallback if PyInstaller proves
+   unusable.
+2. **No code signing for now.** Document Gatekeeper (macOS) and SmartScreen
+   (Windows) workarounds in the README.
+3. **Background auto-update is ON by default**, applied on the next run,
+   with opt-out (flag/env). Also expose explicit `odi update`.
+4. **Binary size: full functionality, optimized.** *It just works* beats
+   *small* (builder's call). Bundle everything so `--backend mcp` works out
+   of the box. Optimize with strip/exclusions. **No UPX** (AV false
+   positives). Because onedir has no per-run extraction cost, size is only a
+   download-time concern. **Concrete threshold (builder's call):** if the
+   compressed per-platform archive exceeds **~80 MB**, add the lazy-`fastmcp`
+   work in Phase 2 *only if* the MCP backend still works in the frozen binary;
+   otherwise keep it bundled and accept the size.
+5. **Versioning: semver primary + release datetime secondary.**
+   Git tag is `v<semver>`; the build also embeds the release datetime (UTC)
+   so users can see *when* a version was released.
+6. **Command names:** primary `odi`; additionally `odipm` and `odi-cli`;
+   keep `agentic-odi` for backward compatibility.
+7. **Wire up the local backend + a `--backend {local,mcp}` flag** so the
+   binary works standalone out of the box (human partner's call; see the
+   correction under Constraints). This is a functional change to
+   `cli/src/cli/outcomes.py` and `cli/src/cli/backend.py`, included in the
+   plan. `local` is the default; `mcp` preserves today's behavior.
+8. **Linux compatibility floor: glibc 2.17-class.** Linux artifacts are built
+   inside an old-glibc container (manylinux2014 / Ubuntu 20.04) so they run on
+   virtually all current distros, not just the runner's glibc (human
+   partner's call). Adds a container step to the Linux build jobs.
+
+## The how (decided)
+
+### Artifact
+
+- PyInstaller **onedir** build producing an executable named `odi`
+  (`odi.exe` on Windows) plus its `_internal/` support directory.
+- Packaged per platform:
+  - unix: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz`
+  - windows: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip`
+- `os`/`arch` tokens: `linux/x86_64`, `linux/arm64`, `macos/x86_64`,
+  `macos/arm64`, `windows/x86_64`.
+- A `checksums.txt` (SHA-256) is published alongside the archives.
+
+### Install layout
+
+```
+~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
+  versions/0.1.0/            # extracted onedir bundle (odi + _internal/)
+  versions/0.2.0/
+  current -> versions/0.2.0  # atomic symlink; flipping it IS the update
+~/.local/bin/
+  odi         -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
+  odipm       -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
+  odi-cli     -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
+  agentic-odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
+~/.config/agentic-odi/update.json   # last-check time + state
+```
+
+- Install root overridable via `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR`.
+- Both `share` and `bin` roots derive from XDG (`XDG_DATA_HOME`,
+  `XDG_BIN_HOME`) with sensible fallbacks. Use `platformdirs` or hand-rolled
+  XDG resolution (builder's call).
+- **v1 is user-local only — no sudo / system-wide mode.** The installer never
+  escalates and never writes to `/usr/local`. System-wide installs are out of
+  scope for v1 (builder's call); if added later, they become install-script
+  managed with auto-update disabled.
+- **Windows:** no symlinks. Install to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\agentic-odi\`; ship
+  `odi.exe` plus `odipm.exe`, `odi-cli.exe`, `agentic-odi.exe` copies.
+  Updates use a deferred helper process so the running `.exe` can be swapped.
+  **Fallback (builder's call):** if the Phase 1 spike shows the deferred swap
+  cannot be made safe, Windows auto-apply falls back to check-only with an
+  "update available" notice, and `odi update` becomes the apply path on
+  Windows. The anti-goal (never corrupt an install) wins over auto-on-by-default.
+
+### Update mechanism
+
+- `cli/update.py` module providing:
+  - `check_for_update()` → query GitHub Releases "latest"; semver-compare
+    against the embedded version.
+  - `resolve_asset()` → map runtime OS/arch to the correct asset name.
+  - `verify_checksum()` → SHA-256 verify against `checksums.txt`.
+  - `perform_update()` → download → verify → extract to
+    `versions/<new>` → **atomically** re-point `current`.
+  - A **lockfile** guards concurrent updates.
+- **Auto path:** on launch, at most one network check per 24h (cached in
+  `update.json`). If newer, download + verify + extract + flip in a
+  background thread, then print
+  `Updated to vX.Y.Z — takes effect next run`. Never blocks the command;
+  network failures are swallowed.
+- **Suppressed when:** not a frozen build (running from source), env
+  `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1`, global flag `--no-update`, non-interactive
+  context, lock held, or install location not writable.
+- **Explicit path:** `odi update [--check] [--force] [--version X.Y.Z]
+  [--now]`. `--now` re-execs into the newly installed version.
+- Updates are never applied to a running process; they apply on next launch.
+
+### Versioning & naming
+
+- Single source of truth = the git tag `vX.Y.Z`.
+- Build step injects a generated `_build_info.py` with:
+  `VERSION = "0.1.0"`, `RELEASE_DATE_UTC = "2026-10-15T21:13:00Z"`,
+  `COMMIT = "<sha>"`, `TARGET = "<os>-<arch>"`.
+- `cli/version.py` reads from `_build_info` (falling back for editable/dev
+  installs).
+- `odi --version` → `0.1.0 (2026-10-15)`.
+- `odi --version --verbose` → adds commit SHA, build date, target triple.
+
+### CI / tagging
+
+- **release-please** (Conventional Commits) maintains a release PR that
+  bumps the version and updates the changelog. Merging it creates the tag
+  `vX.Y.Z` and a GitHub Release.
+- A single **root component** version for the whole repo (one product
+  version), not per-package versions.
+- **First release is `0.1.0`** (builder's call): with no prior tags and a
+  commit history that would otherwise make release-please derive a higher
+  number, pin the baseline explicitly (release-please `initial-version` /
+  bootstrap tag) so the first `curl | sh` user gets `0.1.0` matching
+  `version.py`.
+- `release.yml` triggers on tag push → matrix build → uploads archives +
+  `checksums.txt` + `install.sh` + `install.ps1` to the Release → publishes.
+
+| Runner | Target | Notes |
+|---|---|---|
+| `ubuntu-latest` | linux-x86_64 | build inside old-glibc container |
+| `ubuntu-24.04-arm` | linux-arm64 | build inside old-glibc container |
+| `macos-14` | macos-arm64 | |
+| `macos-13` (or Rosetta on 14) | macos-x86_64 | see flagged wrinkles |

input.content:
# Bundled CLI Distribution & Self-Update — Design

Date: 2026-10-15
Status: Approved (design); implementation plan pending

## Intent and why

Today the `agentic-odi` CLI is consumed by installing the whole `uv`
workspace in editable mode. We want a world-class, "state-of-the-art"
binary distribution: a self-contained executable that a user installs with
a single `curl … | sh` and that keeps itself current without the user
managing a Python toolchain.

This mirrors the experience of `gh`, `deno`, `bun`, and `ollama`: install
with a one-liner, get a native-feeling command, and receive updates without
thinking about it.

## Goals

- A self-contained artifact per platform with **near-instant startup**.
- One-line install: `curl -fsSL <url>/install.sh | sh` (and a PowerShell
  equivalent for Windows).
- **Automatic background updates, on by default**, plus an explicit
  user-invoked update command.
- Automated versioning and release/tag creation driven by CI.
- Support Linux (x86_64, arm64), macOS (x86_64, arm64), Windows (x86_64).

## Non-goals

- Code signing / notarization (deferred; document the workarounds).
- Packaging the MCP server / local server / chat client as binaries (this is
  about the CLI only).
- Publishing to PyPI as the primary distribution channel.
- A vanity download domain (use GitHub Releases for now).

## Anti-goals (what would make this a failure even if it "works")

- Shipping a build that crashes on `--backend mcp` because a dependency was
  stripped for size.
- An auto-updater that blocks or slows a command when offline.
- An updater that can corrupt an install if interrupted (non-atomic swap).
- Replacing a running executable in place (fails on Windows; races on unix).

## Constraints

- The CLI is a Python package (`agentic-odi-cli`) in a `uv` workspace with
  six members. Once bundled, the CLI no longer depends on the workspace at
  runtime; the source tree keeps its current editable-install workflow.
- The CLI defaults to a local SQLite backend (`AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND=local`),
  so the binary is useful standalone. MCP is opt-in (`--backend mcp`).
- The CLI imports `fastmcp` at module top (`cli/src/cli/outcomes.py`), which
  pulls a large tree (mcp, httpx, starlette, uvicorn). `pydantic` v2 pulls
  compiled `pydantic-core`. These are the bundling risk points.
- No git tags exist today; `cli/src/cli/version.py` hardcodes `0.1.0`.
- Reproduction of the current runner matrix: GitHub-hosted Ubuntu, macOS,
  and Windows runners.

## Decisions (made by the human partner unless noted)

1. **Bundler: PyInstaller `--onedir`, shipped as a compressed archive.**
   `--onefile` re-extracts to a temp dir on every invocation and adds
   ~0.5–1.5s startup latency; `--onedir` starts near-instantly. We accept
   "one downloadable archive, installed into a versioned directory" instead
   of "one literal file." Nuitka is the fallback if PyInstaller proves
   unusable.
2. **No code signing for now.** Document Gatekeeper (macOS) and SmartScreen
   (Windows) workarounds in the README.
3. **Background auto-update is ON by default**, applied on the next run,
   with opt-out (flag/env). Also expose explicit `odi update`.
4. **Binary size: full functionality, optimized.** *It just works* beats
   *small* (builder's call). Bundle everything so `--backend mcp` works out
   of the box. Optimize with strip/exclusions. **No UPX** (AV false
   positives). Because onedir has no per-run extraction cost, size is only a
   download-time concern. Revisit a lazy `fastmcp` import only if measured
   size is egregious *and* the MCP backend keeps working.
5. **Versioning: semver primary + release datetime secondary.**
   Git tag is `v<semver>`; the build also embeds the release datetime (UTC)
   so users can see *when* a version was released.
6. **Command names:** primary `odi`; additionally `odipm` and `odi-cli`;
   keep `agentic-odi` for backward compatibility.

## The how (decided)

### Artifact

- PyInstaller **onedir** build producing an executable named `odi`
  (`odi.exe` on Windows) plus its `_internal/` support directory.
- Packaged per platform:
  - unix: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz`
  - windows: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip`
- `os`/`arch` tokens: `linux/x86_64`, `linux/arm64`, `macos/x86_64`,
  `macos/arm64`, `windows/x86_64`.
- A `checksums.txt` (SHA-256) is published alongside the archives.

### Install layout

```
~/.local/share/agentic-odi/
  versions/0.1.0/            # extracted onedir bundle (odi + _internal/)
  versions/0.2.0/
  current -> versions/0.2.0  # atomic symlink; flipping it IS the update
~/.local/bin/
  odi         -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
  odipm       -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
  odi-cli     -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
  agentic-odi -> ../share/agentic-odi/current/odi
~/.config/agentic-odi/update.json   # last-check time + state
```

- Install root overridable via `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR`.
- Both `share` and `bin` roots derive from XDG (`XDG_DATA_HOME`,
  `XDG_BIN_HOME`) with sensible fallbacks. Use `platformdirs` or hand-rolled
  XDG resolution (builder's call).
- **Windows:** no symlinks. Install to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\agentic-odi\`; ship
  `odi.exe` plus `odipm.exe`, `odi-cli.exe`, `agentic-odi.exe` copies.
  Updates use a deferred helper process so the running `.exe` can be
  swapped.

### Update mechanism

- `cli/update.py` module providing:
  - `check_for_update()` → query GitHub Releases "latest"; semver-compare
    against the embedded version.
  - `resolve_asset()` → map runtime OS/arch to the correct asset name.
  - `verify_checksum()` → SHA-256 verify against `checksums.txt`.
  - `perform_update()` → download → verify → extract to
    `versions/<new>` → **atomically** re-point `current`.
  - A **lockfile** guards concurrent updates.
- **Auto path:** on launch, at most one network check per 24h (cached in
  `update.json`). If newer, download + verify + extract + flip in a
  background thread, then print
  `Updated to vX.Y.Z — takes effect next run`. Never blocks the command;
  network failures are swallowed.
- **Suppressed when:** not a frozen build (running from source), env
  `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1`, global flag `--no-update`, non-interactive
  context, lock held, or install location not writable.
- **Explicit path:** `odi update [--check] [--force] [--version X.Y.Z]
  [--now]`. `--now` re-execs into the newly installed version.
- Updates are never applied to a running process; they apply on next launch.

### Versioning & naming

- Single source of truth = the git tag `vX.Y.Z`.
- Build step injects a generated `_build_info.py` with:
  `VERSION = "0.1.0"`, `RELEASE_DATE_UTC = "2026-10-15T21:13:00Z"`,
  `COMMIT = "<sha>"`, `TARGET = "<os>-<arch>"`.
- `cli/version.py` reads from `_build_info` (falling back for editable/dev
  installs).
- `odi --version` → `0.1.0 (2026-10-15)`.
- `odi --version --verbose` → adds commit SHA, build date, target triple.

### CI / tagging

- **release-please** (Conventional Commits) maintains a release PR that
  bumps the version and updates the changelog. Merging it creates the tag
  `vX.Y.Z` and a GitHub Release.
- A single **root component** version for the whole repo (one product
  version), not per-package versions.
- `release.yml` triggers on tag push → matrix build → uploads archives +
  `checksums.txt` + `install.sh` + `install.ps1` to the Release → publishes.

| Runner | Target |
|---|---|
| `ubuntu-latest` | linux-x86_64 |
| `ubuntu-24.04-arm` | linux-arm64 |
| `macos-14` | macos-arm64 |
| `macos-13` (or Rosetta on 14) | macos-x86_64 |
| `windows-latest` | windows-x86_64 |

## Phasing

1. **Spike (highest risk):** PyInstaller `--onedir` bundle the CLI on Linux;
   run `--version`, `--help`, `outcomes add` against both backends. Confirms
   `pydantic-core` + `fastmcp` bundle cleanly and startup is fast.
2. `_build_info` injection + `cli/update.py` + `odi update` command +
   startup hook, with unit tests (semver compare, OS/arch→asset resolution,
   checksum verify, cache/lock, atomic flip).
3. `install.sh` / `install.ps1` (aliases, PATH, completions).
4. release-please config + `release.yml` matrix + checksums.
5. README install/update docs + end-to-end test installing from a real
   tagged Release.

## Flagged wrinkles

- **macOS Intel builds:** `macos-13` is the last x86_64 runner and is being
  retired; fallback is an x86_64 build under Rosetta on `macos-14`. May
  force a "drop Intel Mac" decision later.
- **Auto-update assumes a writable home.** Under system-wide installs
  (`/usr/local/bin`, package managers) auto-update is disabled; only the
  install script manages those.
- **Offline behavior:** auto-update must always no-op gracefully and never
  block or slow a command.
- **`fastmcp` weight:** bundled for correctness; size revisited only if
  measured and if the MCP backend can stay functional.

## Left to the builder

- Exact PyInstaller spec / hidden-import hooks and exclusion list.
- Exact `platformdirs` vs hand-rolled XDG resolution.
- Exact lockfile mechanism (file lock vs atomic O_EXCL).
- Windows deferred-swap implementation details.
- release-please configuration specifics.

## Assumptions confirmed by the human partner

1. Keep `agentic-odi` as an alias alongside `odi` / `odipm` / `odi-cli`.
2. Release assets live on GitHub Releases (`alehar9320/agentic-odi`) for now.
3. release-please with a single root component (one product version).

## Questions before planning

**1. What minimum Linux/glibc must the binary support?**
`release.yml` builds on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu (`ubuntu-latest` = 24.04, glibc 2.39; the arm runner is 24.04-only). PyInstaller does no manylinux-style compatibility, so a plain runner build will fail on Debian 12 (glibc 2.36), Ubuntu 22.04, and most current distros. Wrong guess = the headline Linux artifact doesn't run for much of the install base, and the fix changes the whole Linux matrix (manylinux/older-glibc container job on the runner, or an explicit documented glibc floor).

**2. Is wiring the local backend actually in scope?**
The design states "The CLI defaults to a local SQLite backend (`AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND=local`), so the binary is useful standalone" and the spike runs `outcomes add` "against both backends" / references `--backend mcp`. Wrong guess = either the plan omits a functional change needed for the spike and the "useful standalone" claim, or it schedules a breaking behavior change to existing `outcomes` commands the human didn't intend.

**3. What size is "egregious"?**
Decision 4 defers lazy `fastmcp` import "only if measured size is egregious" — undefined. A full fastmcp+pydantic-core+uvicorn onedir will likely be ~80–150 MB compressed. If there's a ceiling (one-liner UX, corporate proxies), phase 1 must include the lazy-import work and MCP-keeps-working validation; if not, the plan skips it entirely. I can't pick the threshold myself.

**4. What's the first released version, given no tags exist?**
`version.py` and both pyprojects say `0.1.0`, but release-please with no prior tag will derive its first PR from conventional-commit history (likely → 0.2.0), and the first `curl | sh` user sees whatever that tag is. Wrong guess = mismatched first artifact/changelog/version fallback, or release-please config (`version-file`, `bootstrap-sha`) anchored to the wrong baseline.

**5. Does `install.sh` need a sudo/system-wide mode?**
The flagged wrinkle says system-wide installs (`/usr/local/bin`, package managers) are managed "only by the install script" — implying the script can install there — but layout, PATH editing, and auto-update-disable detection differ sharply from user-local `~/.local`. Wrong guess = install script redesigned after the fact, or users can't get the system-wide path the design promises them.

**6. Is Windows acceptable for v1 with explicit `odi update` only, if the deferred swap can't be made safe?**
Auto-update-on-by-default is decided, but the Windows deferred-helper mechanism is the riskiest unproven piece and the anti-goals treat corrupted installs as failure. No fallback is stated. Wrong guess = either v1 ships a risky Windows updater, or a lot of Windows-specific plan work is cut without the human's sign-off.

options.description: Build Linux artifacts inside a manylinux2014/Ubuntu 20.04 container (glibc 2.17–2.31) so they run on virtually all current distros. Adds a container step to the Linux build jobs.

options.label: Build on ubuntu-latest, document floor
options.description: Use the plain runner (glibc 2.39) and document that only very recent distros are supported. Simplest CI, narrower reach.

<skill_content name="writing-plans">
# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

"""Tests for Customer Outcomes CLI."""

from __future__ import annotations

from unittest.mock import patch

from typer.testing import CliRunner

from cli.cli import app


def _strip_ansi(text: str) -> str:
    import re

    return re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m").sub("", text)


def test_outcomes_help_shows_subcommands():
    runner = CliRunner()
    result = runner.invoke(app, ["outcomes", "--help"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    output = _strip_ansi(result.output)
    assert "outcomes" in output.lower() or "outcomes" in output


def test_outcomes_add_calls_mcp():
    runner = CliRunner()
    with patch("cli.outcomes._call_mcp") as mock_call:
        mock_call.return_value = "Customer outcome created successfully: {}"
        result = runner.invoke(
            app,
            [
                "outcomes",
                "add",
                "--job-id",
                "job-1",
                "--direction",
                "minimize",
                "--unit",
                "time",
                "--object",
                "to setup",
                "--statement",
                "Minimize time to setup",
                "--importance",
                "8.5",
                "--satisfaction",
                "4.0",
                "--category",
                "cost_reduction",
                "--business-statement",
                "Saves hours",
            ],
        )
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    mock_call.assert_called_once()


def test_score_calls_mcp():
    runner = CliRunner()
    with patch("cli.outcomes._call_mcp") as mock_call:
        mock_call.return_value = "Opportunity Score = 14.00"
        result = runner.invoke(app, ["outcomes", "score", "8", "2"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    mock_call.assert_called_once()


def test_outcomes_list_calls_mcp_with_args():
    from unittest.mock import patch

    from typer.testing import CliRunner

    from cli.cli import app

    runner = CliRunner()
    with patch("cli.outcomes._call_mcp") as mock_call:
        mock_call.return_value = "[]"
        runner.invoke(app, ["outcomes", "list", "--job-id", "job-1"])
    mock_call.assert_called_once()

# Bundled CLI Distribution & Self-Update Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Ship `odi` as a self-contained per-platform binary installed via `curl … | sh`, with background auto-update and an explicit `odi update`, driven by an automated tag/release pipeline.

**Architecture:** PyInstaller `--onedir` bundles the CLI plus its interpreter and dependency tree into a versioned directory; a small updater module downloads and atomically swaps a `current` symlink to a new version. release-please tags releases and a GitHub Actions matrix builds/attaches the archives.

**Tech Stack:** Python 3.10+, Typer, pydantic v2, fastmcp, PyInstaller, uv, GitHub Actions, release-please.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-15-cli-bundled-distribution-design.md`

## Global Constraints

- Python `>= 3.10` (workspace `requires-python`); CLI package `agentic-odi-cli`, entry `cli.cli:app`.
- Binary/primary command name `odi`; aliases `odipm`, `odi-cli`, and legacy `agentic-odi`.
- Versioning: **semver primary, release datetime secondary**. Tag `v<semver>`; embed `VERSION` and `RELEASE_DATE_UTC`.
- First released version is **`0.1.0`**.
- Install layout under `~/.local/share/agentic-odi/` (`versions/<v>`, `current` symlink); config/state under `~/.config/agentic-odi/`; bin dir `~/.local/bin`. All overridable via XDG env vars; install root also via `AGENTIC_ODI_INSTALL_DIR`.
- **User-local install only** — the installer never escalates; no `/usr/local`, no sudo.
- Auto-update is **on by default**, applies on next run, at most one check per 24h.
- Update opt-outs: `--no-update` flag and env `AGENTIC_ODI_NO_UPDATE=1`. Auto-update is disabled for non-frozen (source) runs and non-writable install dirs.
- Linux artifacts target **glibc 2.17-class** (build in a manylinux2014 / Ubuntu 20.04 container).
- **No UPX. No code signing** (v1). Bundle full functionality so `--backend mcp` works.
- Artifact names: `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz` (unix) / `odi_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip` (windows). `os`/`arch` ∈ {`linux`,`macos`,`windows`} × {`x86_64`,`arm64`}. A `checksums.txt` (SHA-256) ships alongside.
- `local` backend is the CLI default; `mcp` preserves prior behavior (env `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL`, default `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
- Repo `alehar9320/agentic-odi`; releases from GitHub Releases.

## Review Focus

Uncovered inputs/conditions most likely to bite a user — each has a test in the task that owns the code:

1. **Offline / network failure during update** — the command still runs; update silently no-ops. (Task 5)
2. **Checksum mismatch / truncated download** — install is never corrupted; update aborts. (Task 4)
3. **Interrupted swap** — `current` always points at a complete version dir; no partial state. (Task 4)
4. **Non-writable install dir** — auto-update disables gracefully instead of erroring. (Task 5)
5. **`odi update` on a source (non-frozen) install** — clear message, no crash, non-zero-free. (Task 6)
6. **Concurrent invocations** — only one update proceeds; the other skips. (Task 4)
7. **Local backend DB path** — directory is created on first write. (Task 3)

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `update.py`**

- `parse_version` strips a leading `v`, splits on `.`, takes first three ints.
- `is_newer` compares tuples.
- `asset_name` uses `.zip` for `os_name == "windows"`, else `.tar.gz`.
- `current_platform`: map `platform.system()` (`Linux`→`linux`, `Darwin`→`macos`, `Windows`→`windows`) and `platform.machine()` (`x86_64`/`AMD64`→`x86_64`, `arm64`/`aarch64`→`arm64`).
- `verify_checksum` streams the file through `hashlib.sha256` and compares case-insensitively.
- `extract_archive`: `tarfile` for `.tar.gz`, `zipfile` for `.zip`; extract into a temp dir **inside** `install_root/versions/` then `os.replace` to the final `versions/<version>` (so a crashed extract never leaves a partial `versions/<version>`).
- `perform_update`: verify checksum (raise `UpdateError` on mismatch), extract, then atomically flip: create `current.tmp` symlink → `os.replace("current.tmp", "current")`. On Windows, copy the version dir instead of symlinking and record the path in a `current` marker file.
- Serialize mutating work behind a lock file `install_root/.update.lock` created with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`; if held, raise `UpdateError("update already in progress")`.

The LocalBackend compute_opportunity returns `f"Opportunity score: {score:.2f}"`. Good, my test asserts "Opportunity score" in output. 

Now there's a concern: in Task 3, the `--backend` global option. Typer callback options: the root callback `main` currently only has `version`. Adding `--backend` there means it's a global option. But the existing test `test_outcomes_add_calls_mcp` patches `cli.outcomes._call_mcp`. With `--backend mcp` set via env, `get_backend(mcp_url=...)` → MCPBackend → calls `from cli.outcomes import _call_mcp`. Good.

--- docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-15-cli-odi-entity-parity.md	
+++ docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-15-cli-odi-entity-parity.md	
@@ -0,0 +1,949 @@
+# CLI ODI Entity Parity & Shared Store Implementation Plan
+
+> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
+
+**Goal:** Give the `agentic-odi` CLI full create/read/update/delete access to every ODI entity (Job, Step, Desired Outcome, Customer Outcome incl. `value_metrics`), matching the MCP tool surface, backed by one persistent SQLite store shared by the CLI and the MCP server.
+
+**Architecture:** Extend the `core` repository/service layers with CRUD + cascade delete + FK validation for `Job`/`Step`/`Outcome`. Make `SQLiteRepository` read-through (replays new events before reads) so concurrent processes converge. Add a `build_repository()` factory. The MCP server selects that factory instead of `InMemoryRepository`. The CLI gains a global `--backend/--db/--mcp-url` resolved through a shared `Backend` abstraction, plus new command groups whose names reserve `outcomes` for the desired-outcome entity.
+
+**Tech Stack:** Python 3.10+, Typer, Pydantic v2, FastMCP, SQLite (`IntentStore` append-only event log, WAL), pytest/pytest-asyncio, ruff, mypy.
+
+**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-15-cli-odi-entity-parity-design.md`
+
+## Global Constraints
+
+- Python `>=3.10`; every project targets `py310`, ruff line-length 100.
+- Ruff select: `["E4", "E7", "E9", "F", "I", "UP", "B", "BLE"]`.
+- Opportunity Score formula: `importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0)` — reuse `compute_opportunity_score`.
+- `importance`/`satisfaction` valid range is `1.0`–`10.0`.
+- Store path env var: `AGENTIC_ODI_DB`; default `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`; value `:memory:` means in-memory.
+- CLI backend env var: `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND`; default `local`.
+- Command vocabulary: `jobs`, `steps`, `outcomes` (Desired Outcome), `customer-outcomes` (Customer Outcome), top-level `score`.
+- No CLI alias preserving the old `outcomes` = Customer Outcome meaning.
+- Deleting a Job cascades to its Steps, Outcomes, Customer Outcomes; deleting a Step cascades to Outcomes/Customer Outcomes bound to it. Creating a Step/Outcome/Customer Outcome under an unknown `job_id`/`step_id` is rejected.
+- Updates use the `is not None` sentinel convention: a field is never cleared by passing null; `job_id` is immutable.
+- Tests must never touch the real `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`.
+- Run all tests via `uv run --directory <pkg> pytest`; lint/type via the README commands.
+
+## Review Focus
+
+These are the failure modes most likely to bite a user; each has its test pinned in the owning task.
+
+1. **Concurrent writer visibility** — a CLI `local` write while the MCP server is running must be visible to the server's next read (Task 3, 5).
+2. **Cascade delete replay** — deleting a Job then restarting must not resurrect its dependents; a cascaded id reads as not-found (Task 1, 3).
+3. **Stored opportunity score on update** — updating only `importance` recomputes `opportunity_score`; clearing either score sets it to `None` (Task 2, 3).

+# CLI ODI Entity Parity & Shared Store — Design
+
+Date: 2026-10-15
+Status: Draft (design); builder check + implementation plan pending
+
+## Intent and why
+
+A Product Manager (or an AI agent acting for them) should be able to run the
+**entire** Outcome-Driven Innovation loop from the `agentic-odi` CLI: capture
+Jobs, break them into Job-Map Steps, record Desired Outcomes with importance
+and satisfaction, compute Opportunity Scores, and link outcomes to business
+value via Customer Outcomes. Today the CLI only exposes Customer Outcomes, and
+it writes to the MCP server's **in-memory** repository, so nothing survives a
+restart and Jobs/Steps/Desired Outcomes are unreachable from the terminal at
+all.
+
+The objective is to help the PM **think in outcomes, not solutions**. The tool
+must make the framework's core concept — the desired outcome — the obvious
+center of gravity, and it must accumulate the PM's and the agent's thinking in
+one durable place.
+
+Two entry paths must converge on the same data:
+
+- the PM typing at the terminal (CLI, `local` backend), and
+- the AI agent calling tools over MCP (`mcp` server).
+
+## Goals
+
+- CLI input and output (create, list, get, update, delete) for **every** ODI
+  entity the domain models: `Job`, `Step`, `Outcome` (desired outcome), and
+  `CustomerOutcome` (including nested `value_metrics`).
+- **Full parity** between the CLI and the MCP tool surface: anything a PM can
+  do by hand, the agent can do over MCP, and vice versa.
+- **One persistent store** shared by the CLI and the MCP server, so data
+  survives restarts and both paths see each other's writes.
+- Vocabulary a PM already holds: the word *outcome* means the framework's
+  desired outcome, with no second competing meaning.
+
+## Non-goals
+
+- Replacing or redesigning the Streamlit "Living Studio" GUI.
+- Changing the ODI domain model itself (fields, scoring formula, enums).
+- The bundled-binary distribution and self-update work (see the separate
+  `2026-10-15-cli-bundled-distribution-design.md`); this design must not
+  conflict with it but does not implement it.
+- Multi-user auth, remote/hosted storage, or sync beyond a single local
+  SQLite file.
+
+## Anti-goals (would make this a failure even if it "works")
+
+- A CLI that reports success while the agent (or a second terminal) can't see
+  the data, or loses it on restart.
+- Two commands whose names both suggest "outcome", forcing the user to
+  remember an internal distinction.
+- Breaking the live GUI/agent path silently.
+- A test suite that writes to the user's real `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`.

+  Score. `SQLiteRepository` already persists Job/Step/Outcome/CustomerOutcome

+  in `cli/cli.py`.
+- Cross-process sharing must work while the long-running MCP server is up and
+  a short-lived CLI process writes concurrently (SQLite WAL allows this).
+- CI runs `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, per-project `mypy`, per-project
+  `pytest`, and `bandit`.
+
+## The how (decided with the human partner)
+
+### Vocabulary / command surface
+
+Chosen per the "one obvious meaning per word" directive — the framework's
+central entity gets the plain word:
+
+| Concept | Model | CLI group |
+|---|---|---|
+| Job | `Job` | `jobs` |
+| Job-Map Step | `Step` | `steps` |
+| Desired Outcome | `Outcome` | `outcomes` |
+| Customer Outcome | `CustomerOutcome` | `customer-outcomes` |
+| Opportunity Score | `compute_opportunity_score` | top-level `score` |
+
+The existing `outcomes` group (today's Customer Outcome) is **renamed** to
+`customer-outcomes`, and `outcomes` is reassigned to the desired-outcome

+
+Every group gets full CRUD: `add`, `list`, `get <id>`, `update <id>`,
+`delete <id> [-y/--yes]`.
+

+
+`ValueMetric` is nested in `CustomerValue` (inside `CustomerOutcome`); it is

+
+- input: a repeatable `--value-metric '<json>'` option, each a JSON object with

+- output: nested under `customer_value.value_metrics`, each with its computed
+  `opportunity_score`.
+
+This mirrors how MCP already accepts `customer_value` as a dict.
+

+- Both the MCP server and the CLI `local` backend use `SQLiteRepository`
+  against the same path: `AGENTIC_ODI_DB`, defaulting to
+  `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`.

+  select its repository at startup via a `build_repository()` factory in

+  never re-reads the file, a long-running server would miss writes made by a

+  is refactored into a single `_apply_event` used by both initial load and
+  incremental sync.
+

+- A global `--backend local|mcp` option plus the existing

+  distribution design). `--db PATH` overrides the store path.
+- All entity commands route through `backend.get_backend(...)`. The `outcomes`
+  commands currently hardcode `mcp` and will be corrected.
+- `LocalBackend.call` implements every tool name; `MCPBackend.call` already
+  passes through to the server.

+### Full parity (decided)
+
+The MCP server gains tools it lacks today so the agent matches the CLI:
+`get_step`, `get_outcome`, and `update`/`delete` for Job, Step, and Outcome.
+`update_customer_outcome` gains the ability to replace `value_metrics`.
+
+## Verification / acceptance
+
+The explicit "successfully stored data types" criterion is tested by a
+round-trip: through `LocalBackend`, create each entity type (including nested
+`value_metrics`), then open a **fresh** `SQLiteRepository` on the same path and
+assert every field — including computed `opportunity_score` values — survives.
+
+Additional tests:

+- CLI input and output for each group (mirroring `cli/tests/test_outcomes_cli.py`).
+- Backend routing: default `local`, and `--backend mcp` still reaches the
+  MCP tool path.
+- Core service/repository CRUD for Job/Step/Outcome.
+- MCP tool parity for the new tools.
+- MCP test suite isolated from the real DB via the in-memory store option.
+
+Quality gates: `uv run ruff check .`, `uv run ruff format --check .`,
+per-project `uv run --directory <pkg> mypy .`, per-project
+`uv run --directory <pkg> pytest`, and
+`uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r core/src mcp_server/src ...`.
+
+## Resolved during builder check (builder's calls unless marked)
+
+These were open after the first draft; a fresh builder review listed the
+questions a planner would still have. The following are settled here.
+
+- **Opportunity score on `Outcome` update.** `opportunity_score` is a stored
+  field. `update_outcome` recomputes it whenever `importance` and
+  `satisfaction` are both present after the merge; if either is absent, the

+  - `jobs list` → `get_jobs`; `jobs get <id>` → `get_job`.

+- **Referential integrity: cascade delete + validate FKs.** Deleting a Job

+- Exact `--value-metric` parsing/validation and error messages.

+- Whether the CLI `local` and `mcp` backends share one code path for output

+- Whether the GUI/agent rename needs a deprecation window (decision: no

<skill_content name="subagent-driven-development">
# Skill: subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are the four named below, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Rulings, not stalls.** A running plan does not wait on a human. Conflicts,
ambiguities, plan defects, a cap you would have asked to exceed — decide
them. The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger as
`Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. A wrong ruling costs rework your human partner can see and undo; a
session parked on a question costs their whole day and buys nothing.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For those,
stop and ask.

## When to Use

    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "executing-plans" [label="yes"];
    "Partner chose inline, or no subagent tool?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="no"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (inline):**
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution) instead of one context doing every task
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality) instead of only at the end
- Costs a fresh context per task and per review; inline costs one context plus one final reviewer
- Both run in this session, share the same plan workspace and ledger, and never pause between tasks
